title: Daily Water Intake: 8 Glasses vs 2 Litres vs Body-Weight Rules
h1: Daily water — the three rules that all give different numbers
description: '8×8 oz' = 1.9 L. '2 L' = 67.6 fl oz. 'Half your weight in oz' scales with body mass. Where each rule came from and what the evidence actually supports.

hero: Three rules of thumb dominate: '8 glasses of 8 oz' (1.89 L), '2 litres' (67.6 fl oz), or 'half your bodyweight in ounces'. They disagree by up to 60% for the same person. The IOM total-water target (food included) is 3.7 L men, 2.7 L women — meaning drinking water is only ~2.5 L and ~2.0 L, close to the '2 L' rule.
body: Daily water intake advice is a swamp. No large randomised trial supports any specific number for healthy adults; guidelines are derived from population surveys. The rules that spread on social media (half your weight in ounces, gallon-a-day) are marketing amplification, not evidence. Here are the actual numbers.
## The exact factors and rules

> 1 US fl oz = 29.5735 mL
> 1 US cup = 8 fl oz = 236.6 mL
> 1 US gallon = 3.785 L = 128 fl oz
> '8×8 oz' rule: 64 fl oz = 1.89 L
> '2 L' EU rule: 67.6 fl oz
> 'Half your bodyweight in oz' at 180 lb: 90 fl oz = 2.66 L
> IOM total water (food + drink) target: 3.7 L men, 2.7 L women
## What each rule gives
For an 80 kg (176 lb) adult:

| Rule | Volume | Origin |
|---|---|---|
| RDA / minimum survival | 1.5 L | Renal load |
| 8×8 oz | 1.89 L | 1945 US Food Board leaflet |
| EU '2 L rule' | 2.00 L | EFSA panel 2010 |
| IOM men (drinks only) | 3.0 L | 2005 DRI, US |
| IOM women (drinks only) | 2.2 L | 2005 DRI, US |
| 'Half weight in oz' (176 lb) | 2.60 L | Bodybuilding forum origin |
| 'A gallon a day' | 3.79 L | Instagram / broscience |
| Endurance athlete on training day | 4-6 L | Physiological loss |

The '8×8' rule has no scientific origin. It appears to trace to a 1945 US Food and Nutrition Board recommendation of '2.5 L of water per day', which included water content of food (~20%) — meaning actual drinking water was closer to 2 L. The '8 glasses' number was a rounding fabricated for public messaging.
## What the evidence actually shows
**EFSA 2010 Panel:** Adequate Intake 2.5 L men, 2.0 L women (total water, including food). Not a minimum, not a target — a population reference.
**IOM 2005 DRI:** 3.7 L men, 2.7 L women total water; ~80% from drinks. Higher than EFSA due to US survey data showing higher habitual intake.

**No trial has shown health benefits of exceeding thirst-driven intake in healthy adults.** Valtin 2002 reviewed the '8×8' evidence and found none. Meinders 2010 meta-analysis: hydration status normal at ~2 L/day for average adults.
## Worked example — body composition adjustment

'Half your weight in ounces' at 80 kg (176 lb) is 88 fl oz = 2.6 L. At 100 kg (220 lb) it becomes 110 fl oz = 3.25 L. At 60 kg (132 lb), 66 fl oz = 1.95 L. The rule scales linearly with body mass — reasonable for aerobic energy expenditure, over-generous for people with high body fat (which is metabolically inactive tissue).

**Lean-mass adjustment:** if body fat is >25%, base the rule on lean mass instead. A 100 kg person at 30% body fat has 70 kg lean; 70 kg × 30 mL/kg = 2.1 L drinking water — closer to physiological need than 3.25 L.
## When to drink more (evidence-based)
**Exercise:** 400–800 mL/hour of moderate training, higher in heat. Post-exercise: replace 150% of lost mass (weigh naked before/after; each kg lost = 1 L to replace).
**Heat/humidity:** Add 500 mL–1 L per hour of outdoor exposure above 30°C.
**High altitude (>2500 m):** +500 mL–1 L daily; altitude increases respiratory water loss.
**Illness with fever:** +500 mL per °C above 37°C for a full day.
**Pregnancy/breastfeeding:** +300 mL and +700 mL respectively (WHO).
**High-protein diet:** +500 mL per 100 g protein above baseline — urea excretion needs water.
## Hyponatraemia — over-hydration risk

Marathon runners drinking to 'stay ahead of thirst' can develop exercise-associated hyponatraemia (EAH): blood sodium <135 mmol/L, causing confusion, seizures, occasionally death. Documented deaths in the Boston Marathon (2002) and elsewhere.

**Practical rule:** in athletic contexts, drink to thirst. Do not weigh yourself and calculate 'I must drink 4 L per hour'. Sodium loss matters equally with water loss; electrolyte drinks (500–1000 mg Na⁺/L) prevent EAH.
## Coffee and tea count

The old myth: caffeine dehydrates. Real data: at habitual intakes (<400 mg/day) caffeine has no net diuretic effect (Killer 2014). Coffee is ~99% water and contributes to daily fluid balance. Same for tea, kombucha, milk, and soft drinks — all count as fluid intake. Only alcohol has a meaningful diuretic effect (~10 mL urine per gram ethanol above intake).
## Urine colour — the simplest gauge

Pale straw = well hydrated. Bright yellow = mild deficit, drink some water. Dark yellow/amber = 2–3% dehydrated, action needed. This works because kidney concentrating ability responds to hydration status; the colour is a real-time bio-marker better than volume tracking.
**Exception:** vitamin B2 (riboflavin) turns urine bright yellow-green regardless of hydration. Multivitamins routinely trip this off.
## The five-second recap

For a healthy adult: about 2 L drinking water is fine; add 500 mL–1 L for exercise or heat. Drink to thirst plus a bit more if urine is dark. Coffee counts. The 'half your bodyweight in ounces' rule over-shoots for most people; the '2 L' rule under-shoots for athletes.

faqs.q: Do I really need to drink 8 glasses of water?
faqs.a: No. The '8×8' rule has no evidence basis. Total fluid (including from food, coffee, tea) around 2.7–3.7 L is what IOM recommends; drinking water alone about 2 L is enough for most people.
Yes. Coffee is 99% water and current evidence (Killer 2014) shows no net diuretic effect at habitual doses. Only alcohol reliably produces a fluid deficit.

faqs.q: Can I drink too much water?
faqs.a: Yes — hyponatraemia (sodium <135 mmol/L) from over-drinking during exercise has caused deaths. Drink to thirst, not to a schedule. Sodium replacement matters equally in prolonged exercise.

faqs.q: How much water for weight loss?
faqs.a: 500 mL 30 minutes before meals modestly reduces intake (Dennis 2010). No magic weight-loss volume; the effect is via satiety, ~200 fewer kcal per meal.
Trivially. Warming 500 mL of ice water to body temperature costs ~18 kcal. Not a weight-loss strategy — one cracker undoes it.
